title: Airspace Knowledge Quiz
description: Test your knowledge of US airspace classifications and requirements

questions.question: What is the vertical extent of Class A airspace?
questions.explanation: Class A airspace extends from 18,000 feet MSL up to and including FL600 (60,000 feet).

questions.question: What type of flight operations are permitted in Class A airspace?
questions.explanation: Class A airspace requires IFR operations only. VFR flight is not permitted in Class A airspace.

questions.question: What is typically the upper limit of Class B airspace?
questions.explanation: Class B airspace typically extends from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL, though dimensions vary by location.

questions.question: What cloud clearance is required for VFR flight in Class B airspace?
questions.explanation: In Class B airspace, VFR aircraft must remain clear of clouds. The visibility requirement is 3 statute miles.

questions.question: What is required to enter Class B airspace?
questions.explanation: To operate in Class B airspace, pilots must receive an ATC clearance prior to entering. Simply establishing communication is not sufficient.

questions.question: What is the standard core dimension of Class C airspace?
options: 5 NM radius, surface to 4,000 feet AGL
4 NM radius, surface to 2,500 feet AGL
10 NM radius, surface to 10,000 feet MSL
5 NM radius, surface to 10,000 feet MSL
questions.explanation: The Class C core area (inner circle) extends from the surface to 4,000 feet above the airport elevation within a 5 NM radius.

questions.question: What is required before entering Class C airspace?
questions.explanation: Two-way radio communication must be established with ATC before entering Class C airspace. An actual clearance is not required as it is in Class B.

questions.question: What is the standard dimension of Class D airspace?
options: 5 NM radius, surface to 4,000 feet AGL
4 NM radius, surface to 2,500 feet AGL
Tailored to IFR procedures, typically 4-5 NM
10 NM radius, surface to 10,000 feet MSL
questions.explanation: Class D airspace normally extends from the surface to 2,500 feet above the airport elevation with a radius tailored for instrument procedures, typically about 4-5 NM.

questions.question: What happens to Class D airspace when the tower closes?
options: It becomes Class E or Class G airspace
questions.explanation: When the tower closes, Class D airspace typically reverts to Class E (if instrument procedures exist) or Class G airspace.

questions.question: What indicates Class E airspace with a floor of 700 feet AGL on a sectional chart?
questions.explanation: A magenta vignette (fading color) indicates Class E airspace with a floor of 700 feet AGL. Blue vignette indicates 1,200 feet AGL floor.

questions.question: What indicates Class E airspace extending to the surface on a sectional chart?
questions.explanation: A dashed magenta line indicates Class E airspace that extends to the surface, typically around airports with instrument approaches but no operating tower.

questions.question: What is the minimum visibility and cloud clearance for Class G airspace at or below 1,200 feet AGL during the day?
questions.explanation: In Class G airspace at or below 1,200 feet AGL during the day, the minimum visibility is 1 statute mile and aircraft must remain clear of clouds.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a Prohibited Area?
options: To protect aircraft from ground fire
To protect national security or welfare
To provide training areas for military
To separate IFR and VFR traffic
questions.explanation: Prohibited areas are established for security or other reasons associated with the national welfare. Flight is prohibited without exception.

questions.question: How is a Restricted Area designated?
questions.explanation: Restricted areas are designated with an R followed by numbers (e.g., R-2301).

questions.question: What hazards might be found in a Restricted Area?
options: Artillery firing, aerial gunnery, guided missiles
questions.explanation: Restricted areas may contain hazardous activities such as artillery firing, aerial gunnery, or guided missiles.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Warning Area and a Restricted Area?
options: Warning areas have less hazardous activities
Warning areas extend over international waters where U.S. has no jurisdiction
Warning areas are only for military aircraft
questions.explanation: Warning areas extend over international waters (3+ NM from the coast) where the U.S. government has no jurisdiction to restrict flight. They contain similar activities to restricted areas.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a Military Operations Area (MOA)?
options: To separate military training activities from IFR traffic
To restrict access to military bases
questions.explanation: MOAs are established to separate certain military training activities from IFR traffic. VFR traffic is not prohibited but should exercise extreme caution.

questions.question: What should VFR pilots do when flying through an active MOA?
options: Obtain permission from the controlling agency
questions.explanation: VFR traffic is permitted in MOAs but pilots should exercise extreme caution due to military training activities.

questions.question: What designates an Alert Area?
questions.explanation: Alert areas are designated with an A followed by numbers (e.g., A-631).

questions.question: Why are Controlled Firing Areas not charted?
options: They are too small to chart
Activities are suspended when aircraft approach
questions.explanation: Controlled firing areas are not charted because activities are suspended immediately when spotter aircraft, radar, or ground lookout positions indicate an aircraft might be approaching.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a Temporary Flight Restriction (TFR)?
options: To temporarily restrict aircraft operations in a defined area
To designate new Class B airspace
questions.explanation: TFRs temporarily restrict aircraft operations within specified areas for reasons such as disaster relief, VIP movement, or hazardous conditions.

questions.question: Where are TFRs published?
questions.explanation: TFRs are published as NOTAMs (Notices to Air Missions). Pilots should check NOTAMs before every flight.

questions.question: What equipment is required in Class C airspace?
options: Transponder with Mode C and two-way radio
questions.explanation: Class C airspace requires a transponder with Mode C (altitude reporting) capability and two-way radio communication.

questions.question: What is the Mode C veil?
options: 30 NM radius around Class B airports requiring transponder with Mode C
The outer ring of Class C airspace
Special use airspace around military bases
questions.explanation: The Mode C veil is an area within 30 NM of certain Class B airports where a transponder with altitude reporting (Mode C) is required.

questions.question: At what altitude does Class E airspace typically begin if there is no magenta or blue vignette on the chart?
questions.explanation: In areas without magenta (700 AGL) or blue (1,200 AGL) vignettes, Class E airspace typically begins at 14,500 feet MSL.
